The bullwhip effect

Where does the bullwhip hit hardest?

The bullwhip effect is what happens when a small change in what customers buy turns into a big swing in the orders going up the chain. It does not hit every supply chain equally.

Here are five pairs of supply chains. The two in each pair are the same except for one single difference. Pick the one where you think the bullwhip is worse.

What you’ll do

  1. 1See what is different between the two.
  2. 2Choose the one with the worse bullwhip.
  3. 3Collect five things worth checking.

Microtask complete

Five things that make the bullwhip worse

The takeaway

The product is not really the problem. What matters is what it lets people do when they order.

Nothing on this list is about how popular a product is, or how hard it is to forecast. Every one of them is about the ordering: how far ahead you have to commit, how much you can hold, how many people touch it on the way, and whether anything is pushing people to order more than they need.

The bullwhip is not everywhere. When researchers compared whole industries, wholesalers showed it clearly, while most retailers and manufacturers did not. A chain that orders little and often, close to home, through few stages, barely swings at all.

What to look for

  • 1 Can it be stored? If it keeps, orders can run far ahead of sales. If it spoils, they cannot.
  • 2 Does the price jump around? Every discount pulls orders forward and leaves a hole behind it.
  • 3 How long is the wait? The further ahead you have to commit, the more a wrong guess costs.
  • 4 How many stages? Each one forecasts again and adds stock again, so the swing is multiplied again.
  • 5 Is supply being rationed? If orders are only part-filled, people order more than they need to get a bigger share.
